item.title: BREAKING: Property industry reacts to Bank of England interest rate hike
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Bank of England has announced its first interest rate rise in over three years, increasing the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. This decision, made by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), comes amidst ongoing inflationary pressures, largely driven by rising energy and oil prices. Whilst the increase was widely anticipated, it has sparked concerns about its potential impact on mortgage borrowers and the wider housing market.

What Does This Mean for Mortgage Borrowers?

Homeowners with tracker mortgages, which are directly linked to the Bank of England base rate, will see an immediate increase in their monthly repayments. Those on variable-rate mortgages may also face higher costs, depending on their lender’s terms. However, borrowers on fixed-rate deals will remain unaffected until their current term expires. That said, homeowners approaching the end of their fixed-rate period might find themselves facing higher borrowing costs when they remortgage.

Lenders may have already factored in this rate rise when pricing fixed-rate mortgage products, but the possibility of further increases could keep mortgage rates elevated. This uncertainty could pose challenges for prospective buyers and those looking to remortgage in the near future.

Why Did the Bank of England Raise Rates?

The decision to raise interest rates was driven by persistent inflationary pressures. The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose to 3.5% in September, the highest level in 11 months and significantly above the Bank’s 2% target. Rising global oil prices, exacerbated by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, have been a key factor in pushing inflation higher.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey emphasised that the rate increase should not be seen as the start of a prolonged cycle of hikes. However, he warned that further increases could follow unless progress is made towards resolving geopolitical conflicts, particularly in the Middle East. Bailey stated that future decisions would depend on developments in energy prices and inflation dynamics.

Whilst the Bank’s move aims to curb inflation, it comes at a delicate time for the housing market. Buyer confidence remains fragile, and housing transactions are already under pressure. Estate agents and property professionals are likely to feel the impact of higher borrowing costs, which could dampen market activity further.

For homeowners and buyers, staying informed about market trends and seeking professional mortgage advice could help navigate these uncertain times. With the potential for further rate rises on the horizon, careful planning and budgeting may be essential for those approaching remortgaging or entering the property market.

item.title: Estate agents brace for fresh mortgage blow as Bank of England rate decision looms
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The Bank of England’s latest interest rate decision, due to be announced today, could have significant implications for the UK housing market and mortgage borrowers. With the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) widely expected to raise the Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%, homeowners and prospective buyers may face increased financial pressures. This potential rise, the first since August 2023, comes amidst ongoing concerns about inflation and its impact on mortgage affordability.

Impact on mortgage borrowers

A quarter-point increase in the Bank Rate would have an immediate effect on homeowners with tracker mortgages, as these are directly linked to the Bank Rate. Borrowers on other variable-rate deals could also see their monthly repayments rise. Those on fixed-rate mortgages would be shielded from any immediate changes, but homeowners approaching remortgage might face higher costs if lenders adjust their rates in response to the Bank’s decision.

Mortgage pricing is heavily influenced by swap rates, which reflect market expectations of future borrowing costs. As such, lenders may have already factored in today’s anticipated rate rise. However, the Bank’s commentary on future rate increases could prove equally significant. Any suggestion that borrowing costs will remain elevated for an extended period could further dampen buyer confidence and limit affordability.

Housing market outlook

The potential rate rise coincides with a cautious outlook for the UK housing market. Recent data from HMRC shows a 1% decline in residential transactions in September, with activity down 4% compared to the same period last year. This slowdown reflects the broader impact of rising mortgage costs on purchasing power and sales activity.

Forecasts from Savills add to the uncertainty, predicting a 1.5% drop in UK house prices in 2027. The estate agency anticipates a broadly flat market in 2026, with property values remaining around 3% below their recent peak. Savills has also revised its expectations for a sustained recovery, now predicting this is unlikely to occur before the second half of 2028. The firm does not expect average mortgage rates to fall below 5% until early 2028, assuming the Bank Rate will peak at 4.25% by the end of 2027 before declining to 3.25% in 2028.

Emily Williams, director of residential research at Savills, highlighted the impact of global events on the housing market, noting that ongoing conflicts and economic instability could prolong the period of uncertainty for buyers and sellers alike.

As the Bank of England prepares to announce its decision, homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to carefully assess their financial position and explore their options. With mortgage costs and market conditions in flux, staying informed and seeking professional advice could help navigate the challenges ahead.

item.title: Rent arrears surge 50% in wake of Renters’ Rights Act
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New data reveals a significant rise in rent arrears across the UK, with nearly one in five tenancies now experiencing missed or outstanding payments. According to figures from Reposit, a deposit alternative provider, 18% of tenancies fell into arrears during the third quarter of 2026, marking a 50% increase compared to the same period in 2025. This upward trend has raised concerns for landlords and letting agents, as 2026 is on track to record the highest arrears rate in three years.

Rising Housing Costs Strain Tenants

The surge in rent arrears coincides with escalating housing costs for tenants. Despite a slowdown in rental inflation, the average UK private rent reached £1,406 per month in September 2026, reflecting a 3.8% annual increase. This equates to an additional £52 per month for tenants. Meanwhile, wage growth has struggled to keep pace, with regular earnings rising by just 3.7% in the three months to August. Private sector pay increased by 3%, whilst inflation stood at 3.5% in September, further squeezing household budgets.

Although more tenancies are falling behind on payments, the average amount owed has remained relatively stable. Reposit reports that the average debt stands at £1,837, only £13 higher than the previous year. However, this figure still exceeds the average five-week cash deposit of £1,258 by £579, leaving landlords with greater financial exposure.

Landlords Face Increased Risks Under New Legislation

The rise in arrears comes as landlords adapt to the Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect in England in May 2026. The legislation abolished Section 21 no-fault evictions and introduced stricter processes for landlords seeking possession of their properties. This has made it more challenging for landlords to address unpaid rent and regain control of their assets.

Ben Grech, chief executive of Reposit, highlighted the growing financial risks for landlords. He noted that traditional tenancy deposits, averaging £1,258, now fall significantly short of the average arrears amount of £1,837. "With the Renters’ Rights Act making it harder for landlords to regain possession, the financial risk associated with tenant arrears has become a bigger concern than ever before," he said.

Ministry of Justice figures also show a 6% year-on-year increase in landlord possession claims in England and Wales during the second quarter of 2026, with courts receiving 23,635 claims. However, these figures encompass various possession grounds, not solely rent arrears.

As tenants grapple with rising rents and landlords navigate the complexities of new legislation, both parties face mounting challenges in the UK’s rental market. For landlords, understanding the financial risks and exploring alternative protection measures could be essential in safeguarding their investments.

item.title: Upfront property information could unlock faster offers, survey suggests
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A recent survey by LRG suggests that providing upfront property information could significantly influence buyers’ decisions and potentially speed up the homebuying process. The research found that over 80% of prospective buyers would be more inclined to make an offer if they had access to key details such as surveys, legal packs, and chain information ahead of time. This shift towards greater transparency could reshape how properties are marketed and sold in the UK.

Boosting Confidence and Speed

The survey highlights that upfront information does more than just accelerate transactions—it also builds buyer confidence. Among respondents, 41% said they would feel more assured about making an offer with this information readily available, while another 41% indicated they would be likely to act sooner. Families looking to upsize were particularly influenced, with 48% stating they would offer more quickly and 36% gaining greater confidence in their decision.

For buyers moving to similarly sized homes, reassurance appeared to be a priority. Over half (51%) said upfront details would increase their confidence, whilst 30% noted it would encourage them to proceed faster. These findings suggest that transparency could help address some of the uncertainties that often delay or derail property transactions.

Government Reforms and Industry Initiatives

The survey aligns with recent government proposals to streamline the homebuying process. In June, ministers announced plans to introduce upfront sales packs, which could reduce transaction times by approximately four weeks and halve the number of failed sales. LRG has also launched its own initiative to provide property information earlier, joining a growing trend in the industry.

Ryan Mathews, group managing director of surveying at LRG, emphasised the dual benefits of upfront information. “Whilst it’s often discussed as a way to speed up sales, it also gives buyers greater confidence in the offers they are making,” he said. “Surveys, in particular, provide crucial reassurance by helping buyers understand the property’s condition and any issues that may need attention.”

Challenges and Considerations

Despite the potential advantages, there are challenges to consider. Seller-commissioned surveys, while helpful, raise questions about their scope, accuracy, and reliability for prospective buyers. Mathews highlighted the importance of ensuring buyers fully understand what these reports cover and how current they are. Early identification of potential issues could reduce the risk of renegotiations later in the process, but clarity and trust in the information provided remain key.

As the industry continues to explore ways to improve transparency, it could be worth considering how upfront information is presented and verified. Buyers and sellers alike may benefit from clearer guidelines and standards to ensure the process is both efficient and reliable.

In conclusion, providing upfront property information appears to offer significant benefits, from boosting buyer confidence to potentially speeding up transactions. However, addressing concerns around accuracy and liability will be crucial to making this approach a success in the long term.

item.title: Independent estate agency develops its own AI platform
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Chartwell Noble, a Central England-based country house agency, has introduced its own artificial intelligence (AI) platform, PAPi, designed to streamline operations for its network of self-employed partner agents. This innovative system integrates four key tools: property appraisals, marketing, business intelligence, and market forecasting. Unlike traditional software replacements, PAPi complements existing CRM and third-party systems, offering a seamless enhancement to the agency’s technological framework.

Tools Tailored for Self-Employed Agents

One of the standout features of PAPi is Pocket PAPi, a mobile hub that equips agents with tools to secure property instructions, manage marketing campaigns, and handle client referrals. Through a single interface, agents can generate social media content, organise photography and video services, commission floorplans, and oversee referral processes. Additionally, the platform includes the Whisper List, an off-market buyer database designed to connect prospective purchasers with properties before they hit the open market. This centralised support system enables self-employed agents to operate efficiently without the need for a traditional branch structure.

AI-Driven Performance Insights

Another component of PAPi, Vantage, merges CRM and marketing data to provide detailed insights into business performance. It tracks key metrics such as enquiries, appraisals, instructions, offers, exchanges, completed sales, and fee income. The platform’s AI feature, Quorum, analyses this data to identify potential risks and opportunities, generating comprehensive commentary for monthly board reports. Additionally, Market Radar leverages over 2.7 million HM Land Registry transactions, alongside the agency’s own data and independent sources, to forecast market trends. These predictions help Chartwell Noble guide prospecting, recruitment, and marketing strategies over the next six to 24 months.

Ross D’Aniello, chief executive and co-founder of Chartwell Noble, emphasised that PAPi was developed to address the unique needs of its self-employed agency model. He noted, “While there are excellent third-party tools available, none cater specifically to a country house specialist with self-employed agents. PAPi fills this gap, providing the infrastructure of a large office in their pocket.”

By integrating AI into its operations, Chartwell Noble aims to enhance efficiency and support its agents whilst maintaining its focus on personal representation and discretion.

item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH: Foxtons revenues fall as Renters’ Rights Act disruption hits lettings business
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Foxtons, one of London’s leading estate agency groups, has reported a 6% decline in third-quarter revenue, citing challenges in its lettings business and ongoing pressures in property sales. The company’s revenue for the three months to September fell to £45.9m, down from £49m in the same period last year. This drop reflects the broader impact of the Renters’ Rights Act and higher mortgage costs on the property market.

Impact of the Renters’ Rights Act

The Renters’ Rights Act, introduced on 1 May, has significantly affected Foxtons’ lettings business. The legislation led to an increase in tenants ending their agreements early, resulting in a £2.7m revenue impact during the third quarter. Across the first nine months of the year, early terminations cost the company £5.7m in lost revenue. The highest number of terminations occurred in May and June, though the trend began to ease later in the quarter and into October.

Foxtons emphasised that the financial impact of these terminations was largely non-cash. Excluding this disruption, lettings revenue increased by £3.5m year-to-date. However, £2.6m of this growth came from acquisitions rather than organic growth in existing operations. Despite gains in areas such as Build to Rent and additional property management services, total lettings revenue for the first nine months fell by 3% to £85.8m.

Property sales face ongoing challenges

Foxtons’ sales business also struggled during the quarter, with revenue declining by 5% to £12m. Although transaction volumes remained relatively stable, the average revenue per sale dropped by 8%. This was attributed to a higher proportion of lower-value property transactions, as mortgage affordability issues constrained buyers at higher price points.

The broader picture for the first nine months of the year was even more challenging, with sales revenue falling by 10% to £35.5m. While acquisitions contributed £1.1m to this figure, economic uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, and rising borrowing costs continued to dampen buyer activity.

Despite these challenges, Foxtons remains on track to meet its full-year adjusted operating profit guidance of between £17m and £19m, as outlined in July. The company’s ability to navigate a turbulent market highlights its resilience, though the coming months may prove decisive for its recovery.

item.title: Former John Lewis housing chief launches consultancy after retailer’s property retreat
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The former head of John Lewis Partnership's residential property division has launched a new consultancy specialising in build-to-rent strategies, following the retail giant's withdrawal from the sector earlier this year. Katherine Russell, who spent nearly two decades developing John Lewis's rental housing portfolio, has established Lived. to advise institutional investors and property developers on residential investment performance.

From retailer to residential property specialist

During her tenure at John Lewis, Russell built an operational platform managing nearly 1,000 rental homes across several UK cities including Birmingham, Leeds and Leicester. She also secured planning permissions for major residential developments in Bromley, West Ealing and Reading - though these projects were shelved when the partnership exited the build-to-rent market in February 2026.

The retailer cited challenging market conditions, including rising construction costs and borrowing expenses, as key reasons for its retreat. Russell's new venture aims to help other investors navigate these same hurdles, with services focused on portfolio optimisation, operational improvements and strategic planning for residential assets.

New consultancy targets institutional investors

Lived. has already secured several high-profile clients, including an undisclosed institutional investment manager seeking to enhance its residential strategy. Russell is also advising private family offices and asset managers, drawing on her experience at John Lewis where she reportedly generated £500,000 in additional annual operating income across three managed properties.

The consultancy will focus on three core areas:

  • Residential operations and property management
  • Investment performance enhancement
  • Strategic portfolio development

Russell currently serves on the board of affordable housing provider Dolphin Living, further strengthening her credentials in the residential sector. Her move into consultancy comes as many institutional investors reassess their exposure to UK residential property amidst ongoing market volatility.

Speaking about current conditions, Russell noted: "While significant opportunities remain in the living sector, the market presents considerable challenges. Investors need robust operational insights to avoid leaving value unrealised in their portfolios." Her comments reflect growing caution in the build-to-rent sector as higher financing costs continue to pressure project viability.

item.title: Rents keep climbing – but warning signs emerge for letting agents
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

UK rents continue to climb, outpacing inflation, but recent data suggests the rental market may be losing some of its momentum. According to the latest figures from the Goodlord Rental Index, average monthly rents reached £1,592 in October, marking a 5% year-on-year increase. While this trend highlights ongoing affordability challenges for tenants, a rise in void periods indicates potential shifts in the market dynamics.

Regional Variations in Rent Increases

The North East experienced the most significant annual rent surge, with prices rising by 14.2%. This equates to an additional £126 per month for tenants, totalling £1,512 over a year. Similarly, Yorkshire and the Humber saw rents increase by 8.7%, while Wales recorded the strongest growth across the nations at 7%. England followed with a 5.7% rise, and Scotland saw a more modest increase of 2.7%. Notably, the East of England was the only region where rents dipped slightly, falling by 0.3%.

Despite these increases, the pace of monthly growth has slowed in several areas. Yorkshire and the Humber led with a 2.1% rise, followed by the North West at 1.2%. However, the North East saw a sharp deceleration, with monthly growth dropping from 5.6% in September to just 0.7% in October. The South West also experienced a similar slowdown, with growth falling from 2.5% to 0.4%.

Rising Void Periods Signal Market Shift

One of the most notable changes in the rental market is the increase in void periods—the time between tenancies. In October, the average void period jumped to 28 days, a 40% rise from September’s 20-day average. This figure is also higher than the 21-day average recorded in October 2025, suggesting a potential softening in demand.

Regional variations in void periods were also evident. Greater London had the shortest average at 25 days, while Wales recorded the longest at 34 days. Yorkshire and the Humber followed closely at 32 days. The North East, which saw a sharp rent increase earlier in the year, also experienced a notable rise in voids, reflecting a changing market landscape.

While rental prices continue to rise, the slowdown in growth and extended void periods suggest the market may be entering a quieter phase. Homeowners and landlords may wish to monitor these trends closely to adapt to evolving conditions.

item.title: New £29-a-month AI service targets landlords who bypass agents
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A new artificial intelligence service aimed at landlords managing their own rental properties has launched in England, offering automated assistance with routine administration for £29 per property each month. Lettance, developed by tech firm Galleon Labs, provides digital tools to handle tenant communications, maintenance requests, rent reminders and compliance documentation without requiring a traditional letting agent.

How AI assists self-managing landlords

The platform assigns each rental property a dedicated email address and web portal for tenants to submit queries or report issues. Using AI algorithms, the system analyses incoming messages, prioritises them by urgency and drafts appropriate responses or maintenance instructions. Landlords retain control by approving all communications before they're sent, including contractor arrangements, payment reminders or official notices.

Lettance also processes key compliance documents such as gas safety certificates, electrical inspection reports and energy performance certificates. The service maintains digital rent records and prepares necessary information for submission to the forthcoming private rented sector database being introduced under the Renters' Rights Act. According to its developers, the platform checks local licensing requirements against 293 English councils, though independent verification of its accuracy hasn't been published.

Weighing up AI against traditional letting agents

Priced at £29 monthly per property, Lettance offers landlords a fixed-cost alternative for administrative tasks that typically form part of a managing agent's service. However, the AI system doesn't provide several key services offered by traditional agents, including:

  • Marketing properties and finding tenants
  • Conducting viewings or property inspections
  • Physical maintenance coordination
  • Legal advice on tenancy matters

Andrew Wilkinson of Galleon Labs commented: "Since the Renters' Rights Act changes began in May, self-managing landlords have faced growing compliance responsibilities. Our solution sits between complete self-management and paying an agent a percentage of rental income."

The service launches as landlords prepare for the phased introduction of the new private rented sector register starting in December. While AI tools like Lettance may help streamline some processes, landlords remain ultimately responsible for verifying all system-generated information and communications.

For buy-to-let investors considering this type of service, it could be worth comparing the costs and features against traditional management fees. Those with multiple properties might find particular value in automating routine administration whilst maintaining control over key decisions.

item.title: Mortgage shock: Homeowners face £5,000 annual hit as rate fears grow
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Homeowners whose five-year fixed-rate mortgages are coming to an end could face a significant increase in their monthly repayments, with some facing an annual rise of nearly £5,000. Recent analysis from L&C Mortgages reveals that the average monthly payment on a £200,000 mortgage has surged by £407 compared to November 2021. This sharp increase comes as the Bank of England prepares to announce its latest interest rate decision, with markets anticipating a 0.25 percentage point rise.

The Rising Cost of Remortgaging

For those nearing the end of a five-year fixed-rate deal, the difference in repayments is stark. In November 2021, the average five-year fixed remortgage rate stood at 1.30%, resulting in monthly payments of £781 on a £200,000 mortgage over 25 years. Fast forward to today, and the average rate has jumped to 5.16%, pushing monthly repayments up to £1,188. This equates to an additional £4,884 annually, a significant financial burden for many homeowners.

First-time buyers are also feeling the pinch, with borrowing costs rising sharply. The average two-year fixed rate for a 95% loan-to-value mortgage has more than doubled, increasing from 2.84% in 2021 to 5.75% today. L&C Mortgages estimates that this could add over £3,900 to annual repayments for comparable mortgages.

Growing Interest in Variable and Tracker Mortgages

As fixed-rate deals become increasingly expensive, some borrowers are considering alternative options. Data from Moneyfactscompare.co.uk shows a notable rise in homeowners exploring tracker and variable-rate mortgages. In October, nearly one in four remortgage borrowers researched these products, up from 14% in February. This suggests a growing willingness among borrowers to take on the risk of potential future rate increases in exchange for lower initial repayments.

David Hollingworth, associate director at L&C Mortgages, commented on the shifting landscape: “When the base rate last reached 4%, borrowers could secure fixed rates well below 4%. Today’s borrowers may be puzzled by the stark contrast, especially with so little change to the base rate. This underscores how fixed rates are influenced by market sentiment and expectations of future rate movements rather than the current base rate alone.”

The mortgage market continues to evolve rapidly, with borrowers facing tough decisions as they navigate rising costs and uncertain economic conditions. Homeowners may wish to seek professional advice to explore their options and find the most suitable solution for their financial circumstances.

item.title: Landlord confidence plummets vs 2011
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research has revealed a significant decline in landlord confidence over the past 15 years, despite improvements in profitability and a reduction in rental arrears. The findings, published by Pegasus Insight, highlight a growing sense of uncertainty amongst property investors, even as the rental market appears to strengthen.

What’s Behind the Decline in Landlord Confidence?

Whilst profitability and rental arrears have shown positive trends, landlords seem to be grappling with a range of challenges that have dampened their optimism. Factors such as regulatory changes, increased taxation, and economic uncertainty have contributed to this decline. For instance, recent reforms including stricter energy efficiency standards and alterations to mortgage interest relief have placed additional pressure on landlords.

Moreover, the broader economic climate, including fluctuating interest rates and concerns over property market stability, may also be influencing sentiment. Landlords are facing a more complex operating environment, which could be impacting their confidence in the long-term viability of buy-to-let investments.

Improved Profitability Clashes with Rising Costs

Interestingly, the report notes that profitability in the rental sector has improved over the years, with fewer tenants falling into arrears. This suggests that demand for rental properties remains robust, driven by factors such as rising house prices and a shortage of affordable housing. However, these gains are being offset by rising operational costs, including maintenance, compliance, and mortgage repayments.

For landlords, this creates a delicate balance. Whilst rental income may be increasing, the associated costs of managing properties are also on the rise. This could explain why, despite stronger financial performance, many landlords are feeling less optimistic about the future of their investments.

As the property market continues to evolve, landlords may wish to carefully assess their portfolios and seek professional advice to navigate these challenges. Staying informed about regulatory changes and exploring ways to optimise costs could help mitigate some of the pressures faced in the current climate.

In summary, whilst the rental market presents opportunities for profitability, landlord confidence has been significantly impacted by a combination of regulatory, economic, and financial factors. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for those looking to succeed in the buy-to-let sector.

item.title: Property income tax changes hits retirees hard
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent changes to property income tax could have a significant impact on retired landlords, with experts warning that rising tax bills may strain rental earnings and disrupt retirement plans. According to Rathbones, a leading investment management firm, these changes might cost retirees thousands of pounds, adding financial pressure to those relying on rental income to fund their later years.

How Property Income Tax Changes Affect Retirees

Property income tax reforms are part of broader government measures aimed at increasing revenue from the rental sector. For retired landlords, these changes could lead to higher tax liabilities on rental earnings, reducing the net income they receive from their properties. This is particularly concerning for those who depend on rental income as a primary source of retirement funding.

The reductions in mortgage interest tax relief, introduced in recent years, have already squeezed landlords' profits. Now, with additional tax changes on the horizon, retirees may find their financial plans under even greater strain. Rathbones highlights that the cumulative effect of these measures could leave many retired landlords facing unexpected shortfalls in their retirement income.

Options for Retired Landlords

For retirees concerned about the impact of these tax changes, there are several strategies that could help mitigate the effects. Firstly, landlords might consider reviewing their property portfolios to assess whether adjustments could improve their financial position. This could include selling underperforming properties or exploring alternative investments that offer more favourable tax treatment.

Another option is to seek professional financial advice. A qualified adviser can provide tailored recommendations based on individual circumstances, helping retirees navigate the complexities of property income tax and explore ways to protect their retirement income. Additionally, retirees may wish to investigate whether incorporating their property portfolio into a limited company structure could offer tax advantages, though this approach comes with its own set of considerations and potential costs.

As property income tax changes continue to unfold, retired landlords are encouraged to stay informed and proactive. By understanding the implications of these reforms and exploring available options, they may be better positioned to safeguard their financial future and maintain stability in their retirement years.

item.title: Council tax premiums having big impact on holiday lets
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent research conducted by Cumberland Building Society has highlighted how council tax premiums and evolving regulations are shaping the decisions of holiday let property owners across the UK. With increasing scrutiny on short-term rentals, many investors are reassessing the financial viability of their portfolios.

The impact of council tax premiums

Council tax premiums, introduced by local authorities in various parts of the UK, are designed to address housing shortages and ensure fair contributions from holiday let owners. These premiums often result in significantly higher tax bills for properties that are not used as primary residences. For many investors, this additional cost is becoming a key factor in their financial planning.

Whilst some regions have yet to implement these premiums, areas with high demand for holiday lets, such as coastal towns and rural hotspots, are increasingly adopting them. This has led to a shift in investment strategies, with some owners reconsidering the profitability of their holiday let properties.

Regulatory changes adding pressure

Alongside council tax premiums, regulatory changes are also influencing the holiday let market. Stricter licensing requirements and new safety standards are being introduced, adding to the administrative burden and costs for property owners. These measures aim to improve the quality of short-term rentals and protect tenants, but they also require significant investment from landlords.

Additionally, some local authorities are imposing limits on the number of days a property can be let out annually. For example, in certain areas, owners must demonstrate that their property is available for rent for a minimum number of days to qualify for business rates instead of council tax. This can affect the flexibility and income potential of holiday lets.

What does this mean for investors?

For those considering entering the holiday let market or expanding their existing portfolio, it is essential to stay informed about local tax policies and regulatory changes. Conducting thorough research and consulting with financial advisors could help investors navigate these challenges effectively.

Existing holiday let owners might also wish to explore alternative strategies, such as diversifying their investments or adjusting rental pricing to offset higher costs. Staying proactive and adaptable could be crucial in maintaining profitability in this evolving market.

As the holiday let sector continues to face new pressures, understanding the financial implications of council tax premiums and regulatory changes is more important than ever. By staying informed and seeking professional guidance, property investors can make well-informed decisions to protect their interests.

item.title: Why more UK property investors are looking beyond Britain
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

UK property investors are increasingly looking beyond domestic borders for opportunities, with many turning their attention to international markets. One location that has caught the eye of British landlords is Nashville, Tennessee, in the United States. Known for its robust job growth, strong rental demand, and promising investment potential, Nashville is becoming a hotspot for those seeking to diversify their property portfolios.

Why Nashville?

Nashville has emerged as a compelling choice for UK investors for several reasons. The city boasts a thriving economy, driven by sectors such as healthcare, music, and technology. This economic growth has led to an influx of professionals and families, creating a steady demand for rental properties. Additionally, Nashville’s relatively affordable property prices compared to other major US cities make it an attractive option for those looking to maximise their returns.

Another factor drawing investors to Nashville is its cultural appeal. As the heart of the country music scene, the city attracts millions of tourists annually, further boosting the short-term rental market. For landlords considering holiday lets or Airbnb-style properties, Nashville offers a lucrative opportunity to tap into this vibrant tourism industry.

The Appeal of International Property Investment

For UK landlords, diversifying into international markets like Nashville can provide several advantages. Firstly, it allows investors to spread their risk across different economies and property markets. This can be particularly appealing amidst uncertainties in the UK housing market, such as fluctuating property prices and changing regulations.

Secondly, investing abroad can offer higher yields compared to domestic properties. In cities like Nashville, where rental demand is strong and property prices are lower, investors may achieve better returns on their investment. Additionally, the favourable exchange rate between the pound and the dollar can further enhance the financial benefits for UK-based landlords.

However, it’s important to note that international property investment comes with its own set of challenges. These include navigating foreign property laws, managing taxes, and dealing with the logistics of maintaining a property overseas. Prospective investors might consider seeking advice from experts in international real estate to ensure they make informed decisions.

As the UK property market continues to evolve, more landlords are exploring opportunities abroad. Locations like Nashville, with their strong economic fundamentals and rental demand, are proving to be popular choices. Whilst international investment can offer attractive returns, borrowers should carefully weigh the risks and complexities involved before committing to a purchase overseas.

item.title: Build to Rent construction plunges 63% as new housing pipeline dries up
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s Build to Rent (BTR) sector has experienced a significant downturn, with construction starts plummeting by 63% over the past year. This sharp decline raises concerns about the future availability of rental properties across the country. According to data from Savills, highlighted by home-moving comparison platform Moving Compared, just 4,696 BTR homes began construction in the 12 months to September 2026. This marks a stark contrast to the 12,674 homes started in the previous year. Whilst completions rose by 21% to 21,979 purpose-built rental homes during the same period, the disparity suggests developers are prioritising finishing existing projects over initiating new ones, potentially creating a future supply shortfall.

Regional disparities in construction activity

The slowdown in BTR construction starts has been particularly pronounced outside London, where activity fell by 78% year-on-year. London itself has not been immune, experiencing a 28% drop in the number of BTR homes under construction. This regional imbalance highlights the growing pressures on the development pipeline, even as demand for rental accommodation remains robust. In Manchester, securing funding for city-centre developments continues to pose challenges, although some projects, such as Royal London’s funding of 173 rental apartments in Newton Heath, are progressing. Birmingham, on the other hand, has seen existing rental supply help moderate rent increases in recent months.

Implications for renters and the rental market

The sharp decline in new BTR construction starts could have far-reaching consequences for renters. Moving Compared warns that this trend may limit the availability of newly built rental homes in the coming years, potentially reducing choice and driving up rents. The platform advises tenants considering new-build developments to verify whether construction has actually begun, rather than relying solely on projected completion dates. Additionally, those weighing up renting versus buying their first home might find it useful to compare the full costs of both options, including mortgage repayments, deposits, maintenance, and transaction fees.

Whilst the increase in BTR completions offers some reassurance, the steep drop in new projects raises concerns about the sector’s ability to sustain delivery levels in the long term. Without a recovery in construction activity, the current pipeline of developments may prove insufficient to meet future demand for purpose-built rental homes. As the UK rental market continues to evolve, stakeholders across the industry will be closely monitoring these trends to assess their impact on housing supply and affordability.

item.title: New report reveals buyers changing their minds is now the biggest cause of failed UK house sales
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent report has highlighted that buyer hesitation has become the leading cause of failed property transactions across the UK. According to data from the TwentyCi Property & Homemover Report for Q3 2026, withdrawals by purchasers have surpassed other factors in causing sales to collapse. Whilst overall fall-through rates decreased by 6.4% compared to the same period in 2025, the trend of buyers changing their minds remains a significant challenge for the housing market.

Why Are Buyers Pulling Out?

Several factors may contribute to this growing trend. Economic uncertainty, fluctuating mortgage rates, and concerns about affordability are likely influencing buyer decisions. Additionally, the emotional rollercoaster of purchasing a property can lead to second thoughts, particularly for first-time buyers. In some cases, buyers may also encounter unexpected costs or realise that their financial situation isn’t as stable as they initially thought.

Another contributing factor could be the competitive nature of the housing market. With multiple offers often on the table, buyers might feel pressured into making quick decisions. Once the initial excitement wears off, doubts can creep in, prompting them to withdraw from the transaction. This highlights the importance of thorough research and careful consideration before committing to a purchase.

How Can Sellers Mitigate the Risk?

For sellers, the rise in buyer withdrawals can be frustrating and costly. However, there are steps they can take to minimise the risk of a sale falling through. Ensuring the property is presented in its best condition, addressing any potential issues upfront, and being transparent about the home’s history can help build buyer confidence. Additionally, sellers might consider working with experienced estate agents who can vet potential buyers more effectively.

Another strategy is to request a higher deposit from the buyer at the point of agreement. This can act as a deterrent against last-minute withdrawals, as buyers may be less likely to walk away if they have more money tied up in the transaction. Sellers could also explore alternative options, such as selling to a cash buyer or using a property buying company, which can offer greater certainty and speed.

Whilst buyer withdrawals are an unavoidable part of the property market, understanding the reasons behind them can help both buyers and sellers navigate the process more smoothly. For those looking to move, taking the time to assess finances, seek professional advice, and weigh up all options could reduce the likelihood of a change of heart. Meanwhile, sellers may wish to focus on strategies that increase buyer commitment and streamline the transaction process.

item.title: Bank of England considers major mortgage shake-up amid house price warnings
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The Bank of England is reportedly considering a significant shift in mortgage lending rules, which could make it easier for some buyers to secure larger loans. Under current regulations, mortgages exceeding 4.5 times a borrower’s income are classified as high loan-to-income loans, with lenders restricted to issuing no more than 15% of these mortgages across the market. However, proposals to raise this threshold to five times income could provide lenders with greater flexibility, potentially opening doors for buyers in high-cost areas.

How the changes could impact borrowers

If approved, the proposed adjustments would mean mortgages between 4.5 and five times a borrower’s income would no longer count towards the current high loan-to-income cap. For example, a household earning £60,000 annually could potentially borrow up to £300,000, compared to the current limit of £270,000. This change could be particularly beneficial for buyers in regions where property prices are disproportionately high relative to local earnings.

It’s important to note, however, that lenders would still need to conduct thorough affordability checks before approving any mortgage. The proposed adjustments do not guarantee that borrowers will automatically secure larger loans but could provide more options for those who meet the criteria.

Concerns over affordability and house prices

While the potential changes might help some buyers access the property market, concerns have been raised about the long-term impact on housing affordability. Charlie Lamdin, founder of BestAgent and a prominent property commentator, argues that increasing borrowing power could exacerbate existing affordability issues. Lamdin suggests that allowing buyers to take on larger mortgages may push house prices higher, creating a cycle where future generations face even greater challenges in accessing homeownership.

Lamdin has been vocal about his belief that artificial stimulation of the housing market, through policies like relaxed lending rules, could worsen affordability in the long run. He contends that increasing mortgage limits does not address the root causes of high property prices and may instead contribute to further inflation in the market.

What this means for the housing market

The Bank of England’s potential move comes amidst ongoing discussions about how to balance access to homeownership with financial stability. For estate agents, the changes could lead to an increase in the number of prospective buyers, particularly in areas where affordability is a significant barrier. However, the broader implications for the housing market remain uncertain, with some experts warning that relaxed lending rules could fuel price growth.

Homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to monitor these developments closely, as any changes to mortgage lending rules could have a direct impact on their ability to secure financing. As always, seeking independent financial advice could help individuals make informed decisions tailored to their circumstances.

As the Bank of England evaluates these proposals, the debate over how best to support homeownership whilst maintaining affordability continues. Whether these changes will achieve their intended goals or inadvertently contribute to further challenges in the housing market remains to be seen.

item.title: House prices set to fall again as Savills downgrades forecast
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property market may face continued pressure in the coming years, with Savills revising its house price forecasts downward due to persistent economic challenges. The estate agency now anticipates average prices could dip by 1.5% in 2027, following a period of stagnation in 2026, potentially leaving values approximately 3% below their recent peak.

Mortgage costs delay market recovery

Savills suggests the prolonged geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have contributed to keeping borrowing costs elevated for longer than initially expected. This sustained pressure on mortgage affordability appears likely to dampen buyer demand and market activity throughout 2027. The firm no longer expects average mortgage rates to fall below 5% until early 2028, pushing back the timeline for significant market recovery.

Emily Williams, Savills' director of residential research, notes: "The delayed prospect of meaningful mortgage rate relief continues to weigh on buyer sentiment. While we don't anticipate a severe downturn, these conditions may suppress transactions and maintain downward pressure on prices in the near term."

The forecast assumes the Bank of England base rate will peak at 4.25% by late 2027 before gradually declining to 3% by 2029. Despite current challenges, Savills maintains that most homeowners have already adjusted to higher borrowing costs, with relatively few still needing to refinance from the ultra-low rates below 2% seen in 2021-22.

Longer-term outlook shows gradual improvement

Looking beyond 2027, Savills projects a more positive trajectory for the housing market. From 2028 onwards, the firm anticipates:

  • 3.5% price growth in 2028
  • 5% annual growth in both 2029 and 2030
  • A moderation to 3% growth in 2031

Cumulatively, this would represent a 15.8% increase in average house prices over the five years to 2031, outstripping both forecast inflation and wage growth. First-time buyers are expected to drive much of this recovery as affordability gradually improves, potentially becoming the dominant buyer group by 2029.

The combination of relaxed mortgage stress testing, increased high loan-to-value lending options and potential government support schemes could help more prospective buyers enter the market. Savills also notes that deposit affordability has reached its most favourable level since 2008, which may support first-time buyer activity when financing costs eventually ease.

While the immediate outlook suggests continued challenges for the housing market, the longer-term projections indicate a gradual return to growth once borrowing costs begin their anticipated decline later in the decade.

item.title: Mortgage rates hit three-year high ahead of Bank Rate decision
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

UK mortgage rates have reached their highest point in three years, with the average new deal now priced at 5.89% according to financial analysts Moneyfacts. This marks a significant increase from 5.83% at the beginning of October and represents the most expensive borrowing conditions since November 2023. The timing is particularly notable as it comes just ahead of the Bank of England's latest interest rate decision, where economists widely anticipate a 0.25 percentage point rise.

Mixed signals in the mortgage market

While the overall trend shows rising costs, some of Britain's largest lenders have recently introduced rate reductions, creating a complex picture for borrowers. Nationwide, Halifax and Barclays have all trimmed selected fixed-rate products, with cuts ranging from 0.15 to 0.30 percentage points. These moves suggest lenders are balancing the need to maintain profitability with competitive pressures to attract business.

The impact of this year's rate rises becomes clear when comparing current offerings with those available in January. The average two-year fixed rate has climbed from 4.83% to 5.97%, adding approximately £169 to monthly repayments for a typical £250,000 mortgage over 25 years. Five-year fixes now average 6%, with 10-year products typically priced at 6.32%.

Remortgage market sees increased competition

Lenders appear to be focusing particularly on the remortgage sector, where competition has intensified. Nationwide now offers a two-year fixed remortgage at 4.99% for borrowers with 40% equity, while HSBC has also introduced selected products below the 5% threshold. Halifax has similarly targeted existing customers looking to switch products or remortgage.

These reductions come despite expectations of another Bank Rate increase, demonstrating how fixed mortgage pricing follows swap rate markets rather than tracking the base rate directly. With five-year swaps currently around 4.62%, lenders seem to have already priced in anticipated changes. However, tracker mortgage customers may face more immediate impacts, with Nationwide having already increased some two-year tracker products by up to 0.10 percentage points.

For homeowners approaching the end of their current deal or considering a property purchase, the current market presents both challenges and opportunities. While rates remain considerably higher than at the start of the year, the recent competitive moves by major lenders suggest it could be worth exploring all available options. As always, speaking to a qualified mortgage adviser may help borrowers navigate these complex market conditions.
